title: Help is strength
hook: depression and trauma are not spiritual failures, and professional help is part of the path

segments.voice: Yesterday, a psalm that ends in the dark, and a lesson nobody owes. Your line was that sounds hard. Did you let one hard thing be hard, with no moral attached? Today, the last day of what science can say. Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

The prophet Elijah is running for his life. He goes a day's journey into the wilderness, sits down under a juniper tree, and asks to die. In the King James Bible he says: "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life." Then he lies down and falls asleep. Some readers today hear in that scene something a doctor would take seriously: exhaustion, fear, despair, a person at the end of himself. And this is a prophet, a man of God. What happens next is today's lesson.
screen: `ELIJAH UNDER THE JUNIPER TREE.` → `IT IS ENOUGH.` → `WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?`

segments.voice: First, what the angel does. Not a sermon. The text says an angel touched him and said, "Arise and eat." There's a cake baked on the coals and a jar of water by his head. He eats, drinks, sleeps again, and the angel comes back and feeds him a second time. Care for the body comes before any word about his calling. Second, what the sciences say. Depression, and the long shadow trauma can leave, are health conditions. Doctors, psychologists and counselors study them and treat them. They aren't proof of weak faith, a bad practice, or not trying hard enough. Prayer, meditation and community can sit alongside treatment; they don't have to replace it. Third, the traditions have said something like this in their own words. The book of Sirach, part of the Bible for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, tells its readers to honor the physician, because the Lord created him. In a hadith collected by Abu Dawud, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells people to seek treatment, because God has not made a disease without making a remedy for it. Fourth, the strength part. Elijah doesn't fix himself under that tree. Someone touches him, feeds him, lets him sleep, and he takes it. Asking for help takes courage. Calling a doctor, a counselor, or a crisis line isn't a step off the path. For some people, it's the next step on it.
screen: `ARISE AND EAT.` · `A HEALTH CONDITION, NOT A FAILURE.` · `HONOR THE PHYSICIAN.` · `ASKING TAKES COURAGE.` · then, large: `HELP IS STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is practical. Before the sit, or right after it, take out your phone and save one support number: your doctor, a counselor, a crisis line where you live, or a friend who always picks up. Give it a plain name you'll find on a bad night. Then, for the sit, put the phone down and breathe, and let your hands rest knowing it's there. If you pray, you can pray for the people who answer those phones. And if you're in danger right now, stop and call your local emergency number. The bell holds the time.
Elijah, fed and let sleep by an angel under the juniper tree before any word about his calling. Today's word.
Your line: arise and eat. Today, check in on one person who's gone quiet lately. A short message is enough: thinking of you, no need to reply. Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Some religious communities encourage people facing depression or trauma to see a doctor or counselor alongside prayer or meditation, and some congregations keep lists of local counselors and crisis lines.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): 1 Kings 19:4–5 KJV checked exact ('juniper tree', 'Arise and eat'); Sirach 38:1 and Abu Dawud 3855 paraphrases fair. No change.

Sensitive topic: Elijah asks to die. The practice ends with 'if you're in danger right now, stop and call your local emergency number.' The app may want a localized crisis line on screen; no number is given in the script by design.
Second teach point ('health conditions... study them and treat them') is a general medical statement with no statistic; confirm the wording with a clinician.

Sirach 38:1–12 paraphrased (honor the physician, for the Lord created him). Sirach is canonical for Catholic and Orthodox Christians and in the Apocrypha for Protestants; confirm phrasing 'part of the Bible for Catholic and Orthodox Christians'.
Abu Dawud 3855 paraphrased (seek treatment, for God has not made a disease without appointing a remedy, except old age). Confirm number; the 'except old age' clause is omitted.
1 Kings 19:6 'a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head' paraphrased as 'a cake baked on the coals and a jar of water by his head'.
The 'some readers today hear... something a doctor would take seriously' framing reads Elijah through a modern lens; it is attributed, not stated as diagnosis.
